title: Pareus: Bellarmine's question is slippery; which freedom does he mean?
source_text: XXIV. Sic Protestantium doctrinam exponit David Paraeus. Nam proposita quaestione quam format Bellarminus, sitne homo post lapsum primi hominis vere liberi arbitrii, in iis rebus, quae pertinent ad salutem, dicit quaestionem illam lubricam & Sophisticam esse, quia, inquit, obscurum est quanam arbitrii libertatem ad divinas actiones velit, an a coactione, a Physica necessitate, a bruta determinatione: qua libertas ultro a nobis datur: an vero a servitute peccati, seu necessitate peccandi ex vitio, vel a dependentia motionis divinae: qua homini in statu peccati absque blasphemia arrogari non potest. In lib. 6. Bellar. de Grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 8.
pass_a_gloss: XXIV. Thus David Pareus sets forth the doctrine of the Protestants. For the question being proposed which Bellarmine forms, whether man after the fall of the first man is truly of free choice, in those things which pertain to salvation, he says that question is slippery and Sophistical, because, he says, it is obscure what freedom of choice for divine actions he means, whether from coaction, from Physical necessity, from brute determination: which freedom is readily granted by us: or rather from the servitude of sin, or the necessity of sinning from vice, or from dependence on the divine motion: which cannot be claimed for man in the state of sin without blasphemy. On book 6 of Bellarmine on Grace and free choice chapter 8.
pass_b_english: David Pareus sets out the Protestant teaching this way. Taking up the question as Bellarmine frames it, 'whether man after the fall of the first man truly has free choice in the things that pertain to salvation', he calls the question slippery and sophistical.

'For,' he says, 'it is unclear what freedom of choice for divine actions he means: freedom from compulsion, from physical necessity, from brute determination, which we readily grant; or freedom from bondage to sin, that is, from the necessity of sinning that comes from vice, or from dependence on God's motion, which cannot be claimed for man in the state of sin without blasphemy.' On Bellarmine, book 6, On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 8.

lemmas.gloss: that question is slippery and Sophistical

lemmas.latin: qua libertas ultro a nobis datur
lemmas.gloss: which freedom is readily granted by us

choices.why: The will's slavery to sin, opposed to the freedom lost in the fall; 'bondage' keeps the Augustinian sense.
